\section[hablar]{hablar — \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} which used to mean \textquotedblleft{}to tell tales\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C06-hablar}



\begin{quote}
Fixed phrases got you this far. \textbf{Hablar} (\textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}) is the first verb you will take apart and put back together. Today: the word itself. Next lesson: the pattern it unlocks.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{silent-h} — the \textbf{h is completely silent}: \emph{hablar} = \emph{ah-BLAR}. (Spanish \emph{h} never makes a sound.)
  \item \texttt{v-b} — the \emph{b} is a soft \emph{b}; \emph{hablo} = \emph{AH-bloh}.
\end{itemize}

That silent \emph{h} is not an accident of spelling. Latin's initial \textbf{f-} weakened in a whole set of Spanish words and eventually fell silent altogether, but the scribes kept writing a letter where it used to be — and that letter is \textbf{h}. You are looking at the gravestone of an \emph{f}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{hablar} comes from Latin \textbf{fābulārī}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to chat, to tell tales\textquotedblright{}} — from \textbf{fābula}, \textquotedblleft{}a story.\textquotedblright{} So \emph{to speak}, in Spanish, is at root \emph{to tell stories}. Notice Latin had a plainer verb available (\emph{loquī}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} which English keeps in \textbf{eloquent} and \textbf{loquacious}) — and Spanish chose the chattier, more colourful one.

That \textbf{fābula} is thoroughly English: \textbf{fable}, \textbf{fabulous} (\textquotedblleft{}story-like\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{confabulate}, and \textbf{ineffable} (\textquotedblleft{}un-speak-able\textquotedblright{}).

The single path you need today is \textbf{fābulārī $\to$ hablar}; later words will let you test how broadly that \emph{f- $\to$ h-} pattern reaches.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablar\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ah-BLAR}, silent \emph{h}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablar\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}fable, fabulous, ineffable\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{fābula} root
  \item the sound law — \textquotedblleft{}fābulārī\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}hablar\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word is \emph{hablar} from, and what English word shares it? (\emph{Fābulārī} $\leftarrow$ \emph{fābula} — \textbf{fable}.) What happened to its initial Latin \emph{f-}? (It weakened away, leaving the written but \textbf{silent} Spanish \emph{h-}.) Next: the ending pattern that turns this one verb into a machine.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hablo, hablas, habla]{hablo, hablas, habla — one ending swap, three sentences}

\label{lesson:ES-C06-ar-presente}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Hablar} is one word. Swap its last two letters and it becomes \textquotedblleft{}I speak,\textquotedblright{} or a question to a friend, or a polite question to a stranger. This is the biggest single piece of leverage in this book so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hablar — the verb and its \emph{fābula} root.
  \item tú \emph{or} usted — which forms \emph{usted} takes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the -ar present tense}]
\textbf{Hablar} belongs to the \textbf{-ar} family. To make the three singular forms you need now: \textbf{drop the -ar}, then add the ending for the person.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{ending} & \textbf{\emph{hablar} $\to$} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
I & \textbf{-o} & \textbf{hablo} & I speak \\
tú (you, informal) & \textbf{-as} & \textbf{hablas} & you speak \\
usted (you, formal) & \textbf{-a} & \textbf{habla} & you speak \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The \emph{usted} row is the same \emph{he/she} form you were warned about back in Chapter 3 — it turns up here for real. \textbf{This same template fits every regular -ar verb}, so learning it once buys you every \emph{-ar} verb you will ever meet.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: pro-drop}]
Look at \textbf{hablo} again. The \textbf{-o} already says \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{} Saying \emph{yo hablo} is not wrong, but it is like saying \textquotedblleft{}I, I speak\textquotedblright{} — Spanish normally leaves the subject pronoun out entirely.

That is called \textbf{pro-drop}, and it is only possible because the endings are distinct enough to carry the information by themselves. English endings are worn down to almost nothing (\emph{speak, speak, speaks}), so English \textbf{must} keep its pronouns. Spanish endings did not wear down, so Spanish can throw the pronoun away. One word, \emph{hablo}, is a complete sentence.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pattern — \textquotedblleft{}hablo, hablas, habla\textquotedblright{} (I / tú / usted)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablo\textquotedblright{} alone, and notice it is already a whole sentence
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you build the three singular forms of an \emph{-ar} verb? (\textbf{Drop -ar}, add \textbf{-o / -as / -a}.) Which one goes with \emph{usted}, and why is it the he/she form? (\textbf{Habla} — \emph{usted} takes third-person forms.) Why is no subject pronoun needed? (\textbf{Pro-drop} — the ending already carries the subject.) Next: \textbf{trabajar}, \textquotedblleft{}to work,\textquotedblright{} straight into the same slot.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Your first verb — putting it together}

\label{lesson:ES-C06-repaso-hablar}



\begin{quote}
One verb, three people, and the endings that carry them. Nothing new in this lesson — only what you already have.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{hablo} — I speak. \textbf{hablas} — you speak. \textbf{habla} — he or she speaks.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can say who is doing the speaking without a separate word for \emph{I} or \emph{you}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole exchange, both parts, without stopping
  \item it again, faster, and let it sound like speech rather than recital
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Run it once more from memory. If a word does not come, go back one lesson rather than pushing on — this chapter is short on purpose.
\end{tcolorbox}
